module_title: Introduction to Black Soldier Fly Larvae

lessons.title: Life Cycle of Black Soldier Fly
lessons.body: The black soldier fly (BSF), Hermetia illucens, goes through four stages: egg, larva, pupa, and adult. A female fly lays 500â900 eggs in dry cracks near decaying organic matter. Eggs hatch in 4 days at 27â30Â°C. The larvae are the feeding stage and the reason we farm BSF. They grow from 1 mm to 25 mm in about 14 days, eating twice their body weight daily. After 5â7 larval stages, they turn into prepupae, which stop eating and seek a dry, dark place to pupate. The pupa stage lasts 7â14 days. Adults emerge, live 5â8 days, and do not eatâthey only mate and lay eggs. In Africa, you can complete a full cycle in 30â45 days depending on temperature. For farming, you harvest larvae at the prepupae stage (around day 14â18) because they are high in protein and fat. To keep production constant, set up multiple breeding cages with staggered egg collection. A simple 1 m x 1 m cage with 500 adults can produce 20â30 g of eggs per day. Store eggs in a humid container at 27Â°C. After hatching, feed larvae on organic waste like market fruit and vegetable scraps, brewersâ spent grain, or chicken manure. Keep substrate moisture at 60â70%âsqueeze a handful and only a few drops should come out. Harvest prepupae by letting them self-harvest into a bucket through a ramp. Use 10â20% of harvested prepupae to start the next generation; the rest can be fed to poultry or fish. This cycle is the engine of your farm.

lessons.title: Benefits of BSF Farming
lessons.body: BSF farming turns waste into money. In Africa, where 70â80% of municipal waste is organic, BSF larvae can eat 1 kg of waste per 1 kg of larvae per day. A 10 mÂ² rearing space can process 100 kg of organic waste daily and produce 20â25 kg of fresh larvae. Those larvae are 40â45% protein and 30â35% fatâexcellent feed for chickens, pigs, and fish. Replacing expensive soy or fishmeal with BSF larvae can cut feed costs by 30â50%. For a small poultry farm with 100 layers, you can save $20â$30 per week. BSF farming also creates jobs: a single rearing unit needs 2â3 part-time workers. The residue left after larvae feed (frass) is a rich organic fertiliser with NPK around 3-2-2. You can sell frass for $0.20â$0.50 per kg. BSF farming needs little water, no electricity, and can be done in urban or rural areas. It is climate-smart: larvae convert waste into protein without emitting methane like rotting waste does. In Kenya, farmers using BSF report earning an extra $100â$200 per month from larvae and frass sales. The startup cost is low: a 2 m x 1 m wooden box with mesh, a few buckets, and starter eggs cost under $50. You can build your own breeding cage from local timber and mosquito netting. BSF also reduces odours and flies because larvae outcompete houseflies. With training, anyoneâyouth, women, or smallholder farmersâcan run a BSF unit. It is a practical business that solves two problems: waste management and expensive animal feed.

lessons.title: BSF vs Other Fly Species
lessons.body: Not all flies are equal. The black soldier fly is the best for farming because it is not a pest. Houseflies (Musca domestica) and blowflies (Calliphora spp.) carry diseases, lay eggs in food, and can spread cholera and typhoid. BSF adults do not have functional mouthpartsâthey cannot bite or eat. They are also not attracted to human food or living quarters; they prefer decaying organic matter. Unlike houseflies, BSF larvae are voracious eaters and can reduce waste volume by 50â60% in 14 days. Housefly larvae are smaller and take longer to reach harvest size. Blowflies need meat or carrion, which is costly and smelly. Fruit flies (Drosophila) are too small for practical harvest. BSF larvae are also hardier: they tolerate a wide range of temperatures (20â35Â°C) and moisture (50â80%). They can survive in crowded conditions without cannibalising each other as much as houseflies. In Africa, BSF is native and already present in many areas, so you can trap wild adults to start a colony. Houseflies are also native but are a nuisance. Another advantage: BSF prepupae self-harvest by climbing out of the substrate, while housefly larvae stay in the waste. That makes BSF harvesting much easier. BSF frass is also less odorous than housefly frass. For these reasons, BSF is the recommended species for waste-to-protein farming. Never mix speciesâkeep your BSF colony pure. If you see small black flies with clear wings and long antennae, those are BSF. Houseflies have grey bodies and red eyes. Learn to identify them so you can remove any intruders.

lessons.title: Environmental Impact of BSF
lessons.body: BSF farming is good for the environment. When organic waste rots in landfills, it releases methane, a greenhouse gas 28 times more potent than CO2. BSF larvae eat that waste and convert it into protein and fertiliser, cutting methane emissions by up to 50%. A single BSF unit processing 100 kg of waste daily can prevent about 1.5 tonnes of CO2-equivalent per year. BSF also reduces waste volume: 1 tonne of organic waste becomes about 400 kg of frass and 200 kg of larvae. That means less waste goes to dumpsites, which are often overflowing in African cities. BSF larvae also reduce pathogens: their digestive system kills E. coli and Salmonella, making the frass safer to use than raw manure. Unlike chemical fertilisers, frass improves soil health by adding organic matter and beneficial microbes. BSF farming uses very little waterâabout 1 litre per kg of waste processed, compared to 100 litres for beef production. It also does not require land clearing or pesticides. In fact, BSF can be done on a concrete floor in a shed. The process also reduces bad odours because larvae consume volatile compounds. However, you must manage your farm properly: if you feed larvae on contaminated waste like heavy metals or pesticides, those can accumulate in the larvae. Avoid feeding waste from tanneries or painted wood. Also, keep your colony contained so BSF does not become a nuisanceâthough they rarely are. Overall, BSF is a circular economy solution: waste becomes feed and fertiliser, and nothing is wasted. It is one of the most environmentally friendly ways to produce animal protein.

lessons.title: Economic Potential of BSF
lessons.body: BSF farming can be a profitable business. Start with a small unit: a 2 m x 1 m rearing box, a 1 m x 1 m breeding cage, and 500 g of starter eggs. Total cost: $50â$100. After 30 days, you can harvest 10â15 kg of fresh larvae per week. In local markets, fresh BSF larvae sell for $1â$2 per kg. Dried larvae fetch $3â$5 per kg. If you sell 10 kg per week, that is $40â$80 per month. You also get 20â30 kg of frass per week, selling for $0.20â$0.50 per kgâanother $16â$60 per month. So a small unit can generate $50â$140 monthly. Scale up to a 10 mÂ² unit and you can earn $500â$1,000 per month. The demand is high: poultry farmers, fish farmers, and pet owners need affordable protein. In Nigeria, BSF larvae are sold to catfish farms at $2 per kg. You can also sell breeding stock (eggs or young larvae) to new farmers. To succeed, keep records: track feed input, labour, and sales. A simple notebook works. Your main costs are labour and waste collection. If you collect waste from local markets for free, your profit margin is over 70%. You can also add value by drying larvae in the sun or a solar dryer and packaging them in 1 kg bags. Dried larvae have a longer shelf life and can be sold in cities. With training, you can produce 100 kg of dried larvae per month within 6 months. BSF farming is a low-investment, high-return business that fits African conditions.

lessons.title: Overview of BSF Farming Systems
lessons.body: There are three main BSF farming systems: small-scale, medium-scale, and large-scale. For beginners, start with a small-scale system. You need a breeding cage (1 m x 1 m x 1 m) made of wood and mesh. Inside, put a container with moist organic waste for adults to lay eggs on. Collect eggs daily. Move eggs to a nurseryâa small plastic basin with moist feed. After 5 days, transfer larvae to a rearing bin. A rearing bin can be a 50-litre plastic crate or a wooden box (1 m x 0.5 m x 0.3 m). Fill with 10 cm of substrate (food waste). Add larvae at a density of 1 kg larvae per 1 mÂ². Feed daily by adding waste on top. Keep moisture at 60â70%. After 14 days, larvae will self-harvest by climbing up a ramp into a collection bucket. For medium-scale, use multiple bins and a larger breeding cage (2 m x 2 m x 2 m) with 5,000 adults. You can process 50â100 kg waste per day. Large-scale systems use concrete tanks (2 m x 1 m x 0.5 m) and automated egg collection. They process 1 tonne of waste per day. In Africa, most successful farms use a hybrid: a greenhouse-like structure with shade netting to control temperature and prevent predators like ants and birds. Always keep your system clean: remove dead adults, clean egg trays, and avoid waterlogging. You can build your own bins from locally available materialsâold bathtubs, drums cut in half, or concrete blocks. The key is to have a separate area for breeding, nursery, and rearing. This prevents cannibalism and disease. Start small, learn the cycle, then expand. With consistent management, your BSF system will produce larvae every week.
